seo.title: The 50/30/20 Rule Explained, With Examples
seo.description: How the 50/30/20 budget rule works, what counts as needs, wants and savings, and worked examples in PKR, INR, USD, GBP and AED.

h1: The 50/30/20 rule explained, with worked examples
summary: A simple way to split your take-home pay into needs, wants and savings, with examples in five currencies and tips for when the numbers don't fit.
intro_html:
Budgets often fail because they are too detailed. Dozens of categories, every receipt tracked, and after a few weeks most people give up.

The 50/30/20 rule is a much simpler starting point. You split your take-home pay into just three parts: half for needs, less than a third for wants, and a fifth for savings and paying off debt. This guide explains each part, shows worked examples in several currencies and explains what to do when your life does not fit the neat numbers.

sections.body_html:
The 50/30/20 rule is a rough guideline for sharing out the money you take home each month, after tax and other deductions:

  • 50% for needs: the things you must pay to live and work
  • 30% for wants: the things that make life enjoyable but you could live without
  • 20% for savings and debt: building your future and paying down what you owe

The idea was made popular by the US authors Elizabeth Warren and Amelia Warren Tyagi in their book All Your Worth. It is now used by families all over the world because it is easy to remember and quick to check.

It is a guideline, not a law. Think of it as a first draft for your budget that you then adjust.

sections.h2: Needs, wants and savings: what goes where
sections.body_html:
Needs (about 50%)

Costs you cannot easily stop paying:

  • Rent, mortgage or housing costs
  • Basic groceries
  • Electricity, gas, water and a basic phone or internet plan
  • Transport to work or school
  • School fees, medicine and insurance
  • The minimum payment on any loans

Wants (about 30%)

Things you choose:

  • Eating out, takeaway and food delivery
  • Streaming and other subscriptions
  • New clothes beyond the basics, gadgets and hobbies
  • Holidays, outings and gifts

Savings and debt (about 20%)

  • Your emergency fund
  • Savings for big goals, such as a home, a wedding or education
  • Retirement or pension savings
  • Extra payments on debt above the minimum

A tip for grey areas: ask whether you would still pay for it if money were very tight. The basic version of a thing is a need; the upgrade is a want. A simple phone plan is a need; the latest phone is a want.

The maths is the same everywhere: take-home pay times 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2. The amounts below are round example figures to show the method, not typical salaries in each country.

  • Pakistan, PKR 150,000 a month: needs PKR 75,000, wants PKR 45,000, savings and debt PKR 30,000
  • India, INR 60,000 a month: needs INR 30,000, wants INR 18,000, savings and debt INR 12,000
  • United States, USD 4,000 a month: needs USD 2,000, wants USD 1,200, savings and debt USD 800
  • United Kingdom, GBP 2,500 a month: needs GBP 1,250, wants GBP 750, savings and debt GBP 500
  • UAE, AED 12,000 a month: needs AED 6,000, wants AED 3,600, savings and debt AED 2,400

A quick way to do it in your head

  1. Halve your take-home pay. That is your needs limit.
  2. Find a tenth of your pay and double it. That is your savings goal.
  3. Whatever is left (three tenths) is for wants.

Our budget calculator does this split for you in any currency and shows how your real spending compares.

sections.h2: How to use the rule, step by step
sections.body_html:
1. Find your take-home pay. Use the amount that actually lands in your account. If your income changes, use a careful average of the last few months.
  2. List last month's spending. Bank statements, mobile wallet history and receipts all help.
  3. Put each item into needs, wants or savings. Do not worry about being perfect.
  4. Compare with 50/30/20. Which group is too big? Which is too small?
  5. Pick one or two changes. Small, realistic changes last longer than a big overhaul.
  6. Move savings first. On payday, send your savings amount to a separate account before you spend on wants.

sections.h2: When 50/30/20 does not fit your life
sections.body_html:
For many families, needs take far more than half. Rent in big cities, a large family or a single income can push needs to 60% or 70%. That does not mean you are failing. It means the rule needs adjusting.

Common variations

  • 60/20/20 or 70/20/10: more for needs, less for wants, and some saving still protected. Many planners suggest keeping at least a small, regular saving even when money is tight.
  • 50/20/30: if you are paying off expensive debt or saving for a home, you might move part of the wants share to savings for a while.
  • Low or irregular income: start with whatever you can save, even a small share, and build up. Our guide to saving on an irregular income has more ideas.

Things to watch

  • Family support. In Pakistan, India, the Gulf and many other places, sending money to parents or relatives is part of normal life. Decide whether it is a need or comes from savings, and be consistent.
  • Big yearly costs. Festivals, school fees and annual bills can be divided by twelve and set aside each month inside the matching group.
  • High-interest debt. If you have credit card debt, putting extra money there often helps more than saving at a lower rate. See our credit card debt guide.

A budget only works if you keep coming back to it. Check your three groups once a month, ideally right after payday. If needs have crept up, look at your biggest bills first, such as housing, food and electricity. If wants keep spilling over, try giving yourself a fixed weekly amount for them in cash or a separate card.

When your income rises, try to keep your needs about the same and send most of the increase to savings. Over time, the split can drift closer to 50/30/20, or even beyond it.

faq.q: Is the 50/30/20 rule based on gross or net income?
faq.a: It is usually based on take-home pay, the amount left after tax and other deductions. If pension or retirement contributions are taken from your pay before it arrives, you can count them as part of your 20%.

faq.q: Does rent count as a need in the 50/30/20 rule?
faq.a: Yes, housing is a need. If your rent alone takes most of your pay, adjust the split, for example to 60/20/20, rather than giving up on budgeting.

faq.q: Where do loan payments go in the 50/30/20 rule?
faq.a: The minimum payment you must make goes under needs. Anything extra you pay to clear the debt faster goes under the 20% for savings and debt.

faq.q: Does the 50/30/20 rule work on a low income?
faq.a: The exact numbers may not fit, because needs often take more than half. The idea still helps: know your needs, keep wants in check and save something, even a small amount, every month.
